title: Interactive Demos for Product & Feature Launches Guide
summary: Interactive demos for feature launches: the pre-launch, launch-day, and post-launch playbook with adoption KPIs and a checklist, from Storylane.
body_markdown:
I'm Madhav Bhandari, CMO at Storylane, and I'll say it plainly: interactive demos for product and feature launches are their own discipline, not a sales demo you repurpose the week you ship. Every top-ranking guide on this topic treats the launch as one line inside a generic use-case list. My thesis is simple: a launch demo needs its own narrative, its own distribution plan, and its own adoption metrics, and skipping any of the three is why most launches land with a thud.


This is the playbook I wish existed when my team planned its last launches: the pre-launch build, launch-day distribution, and post-launch adoption measurement.


> **Definition:** An interactive demo for a product or feature launch is a guided, clickable walkthrough of a new capability, published on launch day across your owned channels and measured by how many people actually adopt the feature, not by how many finish a sales-style demo.


Buyers already behave this way. As one put it: "really seeing how it's used, how it can be used is really the key thing. Just like when we sell a demo, that's exactly how people buy." - \[Product Lead, healthcare equipment telemetry & maintenance software\]


## What an interactive demo is, and why it fits a launch moment


An[interactive demo](https://www.storylane.io/interactive-demos) is a clickable replica of your product that a viewer drives themselves, with guided tooltips marking each step. For a launch, that self-serve quality is the whole point. A typical B2B purchase now involves six to 10 decision-makers (Gartner), and most of them will never book a call to see your new feature.


The launch moment rewards showing over telling. When you ship something new, the people who care most want to touch it immediately, not read release notes and wait for a webinar.


New to the format? Our guide on[how to create an interactive product demo](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-create-an-interactive-product-demo) covers the mechanics, and our companion piece on[interactive demos for a broader product launch](https://www.storylane.io/blog/interactive-product-demos-deliver-a-killer-product-experience-before-your-product-launch) covers the full-release moment; this piece stays on feature launches.


That is the shift I keep hearing from buyers, who describe moving away from a rep-gated motion toward letting prospects explore first. In their words: "in many ways we are shifting from a default to rep approach... more and more they need to do that before they even want to talk to a sales rep." - \[VP of Marketing, educational publishing & software\]


## Where generic "demo use case" advice breaks down at launch time


Most demo advice is written for the sales cycle: qualify, book, present, follow up. A launch inverts that. You are broadcasting to your entire base and market at once, on a fixed date, with no rep in the room to steer, which generic advice ignores.


The result is a launch demo that behaves like a sales demo: long, feature-complete, gated behind a form, and measured by completion rate. None of those choices serve a launch. Here is where the two diverge on every decision that matters.


Dimension Sales demo Launch demo


Goal Move one opportunity forward Drive broad awareness and adoption of a new capability


Audience A qualified buyer and their committee Existing users, prospects, press, and community at once


Length As long as the deal needs Tight, 10-15 steps, scannable


Gating Often gated to capture the lead Usually ungated for reach on launch day


Primary metric Demo completion and pipeline Feature adoption and time-to-first-use


The distinction is not academic. It changes length, gating, placement, and the number you report to leadership. It also runs deeper than the usual[interactive demo versus live demo](https://www.storylane.io/blog/interactive-demo-vs-live-demo) comparison, because a launch demo has to work with no rep in the room at all.


You can see it in how buyers talk about the two. When they picture a launch, they describe reaching everyone at once and getting the product into hands fast, not qualifying a single account. Design for that audience and the rest of this playbook, organized around the launch timeline, follows.


## Pre-launch: building the demo before you ship


The build starts weeks before launch day, and the most common failure is treating it as a last-minute asset. One buyer captured the manual grind this way: "Our product folk currently I think use Loom to do a lot of their demos, like to record them." - \[Senior Product Marketing Manager, enterprise compliance & sustainability software\]


That approach does not survive a real launch calendar. If your product is hard to spin up, plan capture time early, and expect complex, JavaScript-heavy screens to need workarounds or manual assembly. For sensitive internal platforms, agree on access and security ground rules before anyone starts capturing screens.


### Map the launch narrative to a three-act demo structure


Buyers already think about launch demos in chapters: a quick overview first, then the detail. One described wanting a booth-style first impression before the deeper walkthrough. Build the flow in three acts:


1. Problem framing: open on the pain the feature solves, in the customer's world, before you show any UI.
2. New capability walkthrough: the guided, clickable core, kept to 10-15 steps, ending on the "aha" moment.
3. Outcome: show the result the user gets, then hand off to a single clear next step.


A simple way to picture the flow:


Act 1 (why it matters) → Act 2 (what it is and how it works) → Act 3 (what you get)


Keep the story ahead of the feature tour. As one buyer framed the goal: "let's use storylane to tell our product story and how it works and the value not so much as a sales enablement tool at this point." - \[Product Marketing Lead, civil infrastructure & e-construction software\] For more on narrative craft, see our guide on[telling a good product story in your demo](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-tell-a-good-product-story-in-your-interactive-demo) .


### Decide gated vs. ungated for a launch demo specifically


A launch demo is not a lead-gen gate first and a demo second. Reach usually wins on launch day, when friction is most expensive. Use this decision list:


- Default to ungated for launch day: maximum reach, zero friction while the announcement is fresh.
- Add a CTA at the end rather than a gate at the front, so interested viewers self-identify after seeing value, the same logic that makes a[demo-first path convert better than a discovery call](https://www.storylane.io/blog/discovery-call-vs-demo) .
- If you must capture leads, avoid gating in the middle of the flow, which tends to perform worst.
- For sensitive content, use tiered access: open for public material, an email step for the next tier, and authentication for the most sensitive.
- Treat any front gate as a realistic trade-off, not an airtight lock, weighing reach against lead quality.


Buyers are blunt about front gates: "We need to make sure that all the demos are ungated because otherwise... this one asks for email address right away. If I would be a prospect, I would probably just close the window and go do something else now." - \[Senior Technical Director, industrial IoT / OT cybersecurity\]


### Keep the launch demo to 10-15 steps


Launch attention is short, so the demo has to be too. In my experience the launch demos that get finished and shared are the tight ones: a focused 10-15 step flow beats a 40-step product tour every single time, because a launch audience is exploring between other tasks rather than sitting down to study your product. Every extra step also dilutes the three-act story and pushes the "aha" moment further from the viewer's first click, exactly where you can least afford to lose them.


> **Rule of thumb:** If a step does not advance the three-act story, cut it. A launch demo earns its keep by being finished on a laptop between meetings, not studied like documentation.


## Launch day: where the demo lives and how it's distributed


A launch demo that lives only on one landing page wastes most of its value. The teams that get this right map the demo to a launch-day content calendar and place it everywhere the announcement appears. Buyers we talk to consistently rank product releases as a top distribution moment.


### Embedding across launch-day channels


Map each channel to a placement and a call to action before launch day, so nothing ships without the demo attached. Our post on[announcing a new feature update](https://www.storylane.io/blog/tips-to-announce-new-product-feature-update) pairs well with the table below.


Channel Where the demo goes Suggested CTA


Launch landing page Hero, above the fold "Try the new feature"


In-app announcement Modal or banner for existing users "See what's new"


Release notes Embedded inline, replacing text-heavy notes "Walk through it"


Launch email Linked thumbnail to the hosted demo "Take the 2-minute tour"


Developer docs / community Embedded in the relevant doc or forum post "Explore it yourself"


One buyer described exactly this embed-everywhere instinct: "provided it's available or there's an actual tangible feature to share, we could definitely embed like 30 second tours of how it works or what it looks like." - \[Director, Product Marketing, omnichannel retail & mobile POS SaaS\]


### Coordinating the demo with a launch webinar or event


If your launch includes a webinar or event, the demo is your follow-up asset, not a competing one. The live session builds the story; the interactive demo lets everyone who attended, and everyone who missed it, re-explore the feature at their own pace afterward. That closes the gap between a live moment and self-serve exploration.


Give the same demo to sales and solutions engineers as their leave-behind, so the event's momentum does not evaporate when the recording stops. A short coordination checklist keeps it tight:


- Embed the demo on the webinar registration page so late registrants can preview the feature.
- Reference and screen-share the demo live, then tell attendees exactly where to find it.
- Send the demo in the recap email within 24 hours, while attention is still high.


### Social and community distribution


Launch day is a distribution event, so repurpose the demo into the channels where your audience already spends time rather than waiting for them to visit your site:


- Post a short clip or GIF of the "aha" step on LinkedIn and X, linking to the full interactive demo.
- Drop the demo into relevant Slack groups and community threads where users have asked for the capability.
- Arm your team and champions with a single shareable link, not a slide deck they have to rebuild.
- Share a quick internal tour first, so sales and customer success can answer questions on day one, an instinct buyers describe as building a short tour of the feature to circulate internally before going wide.


## Post-launch adoption for product and feature launches, not just demo completion


This is the section every competitor skips, and it is the reason this playbook exists. Demo completion tells you someone watched. It says nothing about whether they used the feature, and buyers know the difference.


One marketer described the shift away from form-fill metrics: "we're only tracking conversions, like actual conversions from form fields currently in Salesforce and Marketo. But I'm going to update it further... to be also tracking meaningful engagements apart from form fields." - \[Senior Manager, Digital Marketing Strategy, open-source enterprise infrastructure software\]


The fix is to instrument adoption, not applause. Our comparison of[the difference between onboarding and product tours](https://www.storylane.io/blog/user-onboarding-vs-product-tours) is a useful primer on the adoption mindset.


### Launch-specific KPIs that beat completion rate


Metric What it measures Why it beats demo completion


Time-to-first-use Time from launch to a user's first real interaction with the feature Shows the demo drove action, not just views


% of existing users who engage Share of your current base that tries the new feature Ties the launch to the installed base, where adoption compounds


Feature adoption rate Repeat use across the first 30-60 days Separates one-time curiosity from genuine adoption


Demo-influenced pipeline New opportunities that touched the launch demo Connects the launch to revenue without a front-of-flow form


Report these to leadership instead of demo views. They tie the launch to product usage, the only outcome that still matters a quarter later.


### How to instrument these KPIs with your demo analytics


Start by logging a baseline before launch: current usage of the surface the feature lives in, so you can measure lift rather than raw numbers. Tag the launch demo as its own campaign in your analytics and CRM, and connect demo engagement events to your product usage data so you can follow a viewer from the demo into first use.


Configure visitor and intent tracking carefully. Identity signals can misfire and mislabel your own team or bots, so validate the data before you build reports on it. If the deeper adoption analytics you want sit behind a higher plan, decide up front which KPIs justify that investment.


One outcome pattern is worth building for deliberately: using engagement signals to surface hot leads and turn a launch demo into[demo-qualified pipeline](https://www.storylane.io/blog/demo-qualified-pipeline) . A live customer described watching demo engagement and acting on it: "what I always kept an eye on Storylane and to see like who was engaging and if I found an interesting thing, I would send them... this is a hot lead." - \[Director of Marketing, veterinary payment/financing fintech\]


## Demo lifecycle: retiring or updating the launch demo once the feature goes GA


A launch demo is not permanent, and treating it as set-and-forget is how you end up with a broken tour six months later. Buyers describe this maintenance burden vividly: "we tried to build out these demos and what would happen a lot of times is new features get introduced and then you have to redo a lot of stuff or functionality changes or the UI changes." - \[Enterprise Account Executive, generative AI & knowledge management\]


Once the feature reaches general availability, the launch demo has to either graduate into an evergreen asset or be retired. Decide which on a set date, not by neglect. A short lifecycle checklist:


- Re-record or re-capture any steps where the UI has changed since launch day.
- Fold the demo into your permanent product tour or a Demo Hub if it still earns attention.
- Update the CTA from "new" framing to standard evergreen messaging.
- Archive the launch-day version and keep its analytics for your next launch retrospective.


## Worked example: a launch demo built end-to-end


Here is how I would build a launch demo for a hypothetical analytics feature, start to finish. It is illustrative, not a customer story, so you can copy the shape. For inspiration from real launches, browse[some of the best product launch examples](https://www.storylane.io/blog/best-product-launch-examples-to-learn-from) .


> **The build:** Two weeks out, capture the feature in a staging environment and script the three acts. Act 1 opens on the reporting pain, Act 2 walks a 12-step setup-to-insight flow, and Act 3 lands on the finished dashboard. The demo ships ungated, with a single "Start your trial" CTA at the end.


On launch day, that same demo goes into the landing-page hero, an in-app banner for existing users, the release notes, and the launch email. A short GIF of the finished dashboard runs on social, linking back to the full interactive demo.


For measurement, the team logs baseline usage the week before, tags the demo as its own campaign, and tracks time-to-first-use plus the share of existing users who build a report within 30 days. This mirrors a real buyer plan I heard: "we have that product release coming up in October and the use case for that is we're launching a new feature and Rocky's going to be building a Demo that our AES more than likely can send to their prospects." - \[Product marketing leadership, B2B pipeline marketing & advertising SaaS\]


## Common mistakes when you launch with interactive demos


Most launch demos fail in predictable ways. Avoid these:


- Shipping a sales demo in launch clothing: 40 steps, feature-complete, and far too long for a launch audience.
- Gating the demo at the front on launch day, which trades most of your reach for a handful of email addresses.
- Publishing it in one place, a single landing page, instead of every channel carrying the announcement.
- Measuring completion instead of adoption, so you cannot tell leadership whether anyone actually used the feature.
- Treating the demo as a one-off asset, when the real return comes from producing launch demos repeatably and at scale.
- Letting it rot after GA, so the tour breaks the first time the UI changes.


None of these are exotic. Each one comes from treating the launch demo as an afterthought rather than a planned asset, which is exactly the habit this playbook is built to break.


## The launch demo checklist for product and feature launches


Run this checklist for every launch. Pair it with[a full SaaS launch checklist](https://www.storylane.io/blog/how-to-launch-a-saas-product-checklist-included) for the broader release plan.


Treat it as a gate at each stage. Do not move from pre-launch to launch day until every pre-launch box is checked, and do not close out the launch until the post-launch items are done. The point is to make the demo a repeatable part of your release process, not a scramble the night before.


Pre-launch:


- Script the three-act narrative before touching the UI.
- Capture the feature and keep the flow to 10-15 steps.
- Choose gated vs. ungated deliberately, defaulting to ungated.
- Log a usage baseline for adoption measurement.


Launch day:


- Embed the demo in the landing page, in-app, release notes, and email.
- Repurpose a clip for social and community.
- Arm sales, customer success, and champions with one shareable link.


Post-launch:


- Report time-to-first-use and existing-user engagement, not just completion.
- Tag the demo as its own campaign in analytics and CRM.
- Schedule a GA-date decision to update, evergreen, or retire the demo.


## Full disclosure: this is how Storylane fits


Full disclosure: this is us. Storylane builds interactive demo software, so here is the honest mechanism, including where it does not fit. You capture real screens from your product, add guided tooltips that turn them into a self-driven walkthrough rather than a video, and publish that flow ungated or gated.[Demo Hubs let you group launch demos in one destination](https://www.storylane.io/blog/multi-product-demo-strategy) , and Sandbox Demos give a fuller hands-on environment for complex products.


For a launch specifically, the analytics are the point. You can tag a launch demo, watch engagement, and route hot signals to your team the way that veterinary-fintech buyer described, turning what is usually a broadcast asset into a genuine pipeline source.


Where it does not fit: if your product is extremely JavaScript-heavy, some screens will need capture workarounds. And if your launch is purely offline, with no digital surface to walk through, an interactive demo is the wrong tool.


## FAQ


**How is a launch demo different from a sales demo?**


A sales demo moves one qualified opportunity forward and can run as long as the deal needs. A launch demo broadcasts a new capability to your whole audience at once, so it is tighter, usually ungated, and measured by feature adoption rather than pipeline.


**How long should a feature-launch demo be?**


Keep it to roughly 10-15 steps. Launch attention is short and viewers are exploring between other tasks, so a focused flow that ends on the "aha" moment gets finished and shared.


**Should a launch demo be gated or ungated?**


Default to ungated on launch day to maximize reach, and add a CTA at the end for people who want to go further. If you need to capture leads, avoid gating in the middle of the flow, and use tiered access for genuinely sensitive content.


**What should I measure after a launch demo goes live?**


Measure adoption, not applause. Track time-to-first-use, the share of existing users who engage with the feature, and the feature adoption rate over the first 30-60 days. They connect the launch to product usage, unlike demo completion.


**What happens to the launch demo once the feature is generally available?**


Decide on a set date whether to update it into an evergreen tour, fold it into a Demo Hub, or retire it. Re-capture any steps where the UI changed, and archive the launch-day version with its analytics for your next retrospective.


## Conclusion


Interactive demos for product and feature launches are not a nice-to-have bolted onto launch day; they are the launch asset that carries your narrative, your distribution, and your adoption story. Build the three acts before you ship, distribute everywhere the announcement lives, and measure adoption instead of completion.


The reason this works is that it matches how buyers already behave: they want to see and touch a new capability before they talk to anyone. The competitors ranking for this topic gesture at launches in a sentence or two and never hand you a timeline, launch-specific KPIs, or a checklist you can actually run. That is the gap this playbook closes.


So treat every launch demo as its own project, with a start date, a distribution plan, and an adoption target. Build the demo before you ship, distribute it everywhere the announcement lives, and hold yourself to an adoption number rather than a completion rate.


Do that and your next launch will do more than get noticed. It will get used.
